JSON: Name: fwist_liquidmetal_handtracking Title: Liquid-metal dynamic wetting-based flexible wearable sensing for spatiotemporal monitoring and reconstruction of hand kinematics Short Hypothesis: Bone-mounted flexible sensors that transduce liquid-metal dynamic wetting in microstructured PDMS channels produce resistance signals that vary deterministically with palm pitch/roll and phalange bending, enabling reconstruction of hand joint angles with median absolute error ≤2° under normal operating conditions. Related Work: Existing hand-tracking approaches include vision-based methods (real-time monocular and depth-based pose estimation) which are vulnerable to occlusion, lighting changes, and ambiguous object interactions; IMU- and magnetometer-based glove systems that achieve high local orientation sensing but suffer from magnetic interference, drift, bulky rigid housings, and reduced wearability; flexible soft sensors (resistive, capacitive, optical, fiber/FBG) that improve comfort but face hysteresis, coupling between contact and deformation, durability under repeated large deformations, and calibration challenges. Prior liquid-metal sensors have demonstrated angle sensing via droplet or wetting phenomena but have not combined microstructured gradient channels, controlled oxide-mediated adhesion, and bone-mounted placement to produce compact, low-deformation, multi-unit arrays for full-hand spatiotemporal reconstruction. Remaining limitations in prior work include limited robustness under dynamic rotation, limited cyclic stability, signal ambiguity across certain angular ranges, and lack of large-scale human-subject validation and manufacturable fabrication workflows. Abstract: Reliable wearable hand motion capture is impeded by occlusion, electromagnetic interference, and signal ambiguity in current vision, inertial, and soft-sensor approaches. We present a spatiotemporal hand-tracking approach based on liquid-metal dynamic wetting in microstructured PDMS microchannels: compact, bone-mounted flexible sensing units (FWIST) containing gradient-distributed liquid metal produce deterministic resistance changes when the gas–liquid interface migrates under tilt and bending. The core contributions are (1) a microchannel morphology and oxide-modified adhesion strategy that yields stable three-phase interface transduction with submillimeter device volume, (2) characterization of resistance response as a function of pitch, roll, injection parameters, and rotational frequency, and (3) integration of 16 FWIST units to reconstruct palm pitch/roll and per-phalange bending for full-hand pose tracking. Expected outcomes are low-latency, repeatable angular measurements with ≈2° resolution, long-term cyclic stability, and applicability to gesture classification and kinematic reconstruction in environments unsuitable for vision or magnetic sensing. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Controlled stage dataset: FWIST mounted on motorized dual-axis rotational stage; static grid of pitch θ ∈ [-90°,270°] sampled every 2° and roll ω ∈ [-90°,180°] sampled every 2°; for each (θ,ω) record 10 repeated resistance traces at sampling rate 200 Hz. (2) Dynamic stage dataset: sinusoidal and step rotations at frequencies f ∈ {0.034,0.1,0.2,0.34,1.0,2.0} Hz and angular velocities up to limits of human motions; 50 repeats per frequency. (3) Human-subject dataset: N=30 participants (balanced hand size distribution), 16-sensor FWIST glove, 8 canonical gestures × 50 trials per gesture per subject = 12,000 trials; sampling at 200 Hz; synchronized ground truth from optical motion capture (marker-based) and a commercial inertial-glove baseline. Baselines: (A) six-axis IMU-per-bone glove (bone-mounted IMUs), (B) commercial optical/depth tracker (markerless, e.g., Leap-like), (C) soft resistive strain-sensor glove. Evaluation metrics: angular RMSE and MAE per joint, angular resolution, latency/response time (90% step response time), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), cyclic drift per 1000 cycles, classification accuracy and F1 for gesture recognition, failure rate under occlusion/electromagnetic perturbation, inter-subject variability (std of MAE across subjects). Experimental setup: Agilent 34420A or equivalent high-precision multimeter, 16-channel simultaneous acquisition, ambient temperature varied over 10°C–40°C, humidity 20%–80%; perform 5000-cycle durability test on each FWIST unit. Comparisons and ablations: (i) Baseline vs FWIST: compare per-joint MAE, latency, and robustness under magnetic interference and occlusion. (ii) Ablation A: remove LM oxide coating (reduce adhesion) and measure change in MAE, SNR, and stability. (iii) Ablation B: replace scale-like microstructure with smooth microchannel (no gradient) and measure amplitude and linearity changes. (iv) Ablation C: joint-mounted vs bone-mounted placement for identical microchannels to compare signal distinguishability and ambiguity in roll ranges (90°–180°). (v) Fabrication parameter sweep: LM injection speed ∈ {0.1,1,10} ms^{-1} and sealing methods, measure amplitude vs frequency and injection-dependent variance. Analysis: compute per-joint error distributions, perform repeated-measures ANOVA across conditions, report 95% confidence intervals, and cross-validated neural-network gesture classification with 5-fold subject-wise splits. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: loss of stable adhesion between LM oxide and PDMS leading to three-phase interface sliding or signal collapse; rupture or delamination of LM oxide under extreme deformation; electrode/seal failure leading to electrical open circuits. Data and evaluation biases: limited subject diversity or hand sizes may bias performance; optical motion-capture ground truth inaccuracies during contact or occlusions. Scalability and manufacturability: variability in hand-cast horsehair replication process, LM injection speed control, and sealing can cause inter-device variability; scale-up requires transition to precision-printed masters and controlled LM dispensing. Environmental sensitivity: sensor response amplitude depends on rotational frequency and temperature; humidity or sweat may alter surface chemistry. Generalization limits: ambiguous resistance signatures in specific roll ranges (90°–180°) may require additional units or classification logic; high-frequency rapid motions may reduce amplitude and resolution. Practical constraints: system currently requires 16 sensors per hand increasing cost, wiring, data throughput and power needs; biocompatibility and long-term skin contact regulatory requirements not addressed.
